Fixes #714.

## Problem

The `/rooms` edge lane serves its stored copy immediately and refreshes it in the background. The refresh fetched the canonical public URL without bypassing Cloudflare's HTTP cache. Because the stored response carries `s-maxage=86400`, that subrequest could read the old cached body, attach a new `x-edge-stamp`, and write the same body back.

This matches production on 2026-09-05: three bare `/rooms` reads returned the same `107961` total while `x-edge-stamp` advanced; uncached query variants returned `109633`, `109647`, then `109663`.

## Fix

Set the revalidation subrequest's standard `RequestInit.cache` mode to `no-store`. Cloudflare documents `no-store` as a supported Workers fetch cache mode. This bypasses the shared HTTP cache only for the background origin refresh; the Cache API remains the reader-facing copy and the existing single-flight/timeout behavior is unchanged.

No new dependency or abstraction.

## Verification

Exact base: `e88db03c79ae0ae1f6bf9bb2e21e5a1ea42dd0f9`

- Regression test failed before the fix and passed after it.
- `node --check edge/src/worker.js`
- Edge tests: **26 passed, 1 skipped**
- Full suite: **667 passed, 1 skipped**
- Coverage: **98.01%**
- Ruff, format, Ty, `sz.py --check`, and size caps passed.
- `git diff --check`, secret scan, dangerous-pattern scan, and unrelated-diff scan passed.

Cloudflare reference: https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/request/
title: fix(edge): bypass cache when refreshing rooms

Resolves #698, finding 1. Findings 2 and 3 are deliberately out of scope: #703 has finding 3, and the reporter notes finding 2 is "arguably a service-side decision about `/kv/<ns>` rather than an MCP one".

## What

`list_notes` was the only listing tool with no bound. `read_room` takes `since` and `limit`; `list_rooms` takes `limit`. Measured on `mcp.technocore.chat` (0.11.1):

```
GET /kv/did   status=200 bytes=3277014
```

3.28 MB in one tool result, into a model's context. #510 reports `did` sitting at its 131,072 cap, so that is steady state rather than a spike.

## Why the bound is not forwarded

`/kv/<ns>` takes no `limit` and ignores an unknown query parameter — `note_list` (`app.py:1710-1719`) reads only `path_params`, and `store.list_notes` (`store.py:2543-2546`) returns the whole sorted list. Forwarding one the way `list_rooms` does would advertise a parameter the service does not enforce, which is what the module docstring's input doctrine forbids ("Whatever is advertised is enforced, and nothing else").

So the bound is applied to the answer, and three things keep that honest:

- **Clamped the way the service clamps its own listing.** `app._rooms` is `min(_cursor(q.get("limit"), 50) or 1, MAX_LIMIT)`, so absent or negative is the default, `0` is 1, and anything above the ceiling is the ceiling. `_clamp_notes` mirrors that rather than inventing a second rule.
- **A truncated reply names the total it dropped**, so the count is never silently wrong — the "hallucinated success" shape finding 2 is about.
- **Only `/kv/`-prefixed lines are keys.** Once the read budget is nearly spent, `budget_note` (`limit.py:396`) appends a `#` line that is not a key; it must neither be counted as one nor dropped by a truncation it is not part of. Pinned by a direct test.

A listing that fits under the bound is returned byte-for-byte as before.

## Judgment call worth flagging

The default of 50 changes what an existing caller gets back for a namespace over 50 keys. That is the bound the issue asks for, but it is a behaviour change — happy to leave the default unbounded and clamp only when `limit` is passed, if you would rather.

A server-side `?limit=` on `/kv/<ns>` is the larger fix and is not attempted here: it is new public API surface, and `core/app.py` is at 1019 of its 1020-line cap.

## Checks

- `uv run ruff check .` — All checks passed
- `uv run ruff format --check .` — 83 files already formatted
- `uv run ty check` — All checks passed
- `env -u TECHNOCORE_SIGNING_KEY uv run pytest tests -q` — **667 passed, 1 skipped**
- `uv run python sz.py --caps` — unchanged from main (`sz.py:44-45` scopes the policy to `src/*.py`, so `mcp/` adds no cap pressure)

Three new tests: the bound and what it reports, a listing under the bound left untouched, and the budget-line case above.

body:
Closes #711.

## The bug

The write side takes a nonce as **1–19 decimal digits of text** — the POST schema says `type: string, pattern: ^[0-9]{1,19}$`. The read side gave it back as a **bare JSON number** — `messages[].nonce` was declared `integer`, and `read_messages` emitted the stored `int` as-is. Nineteen digits is past `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` (2^53 − 1), so a JavaScript reader has rounded the value before it can rebuild `room|nonce|text`, and the record it just read cannot re-verify from the view it was read from.

Not theoretical. From today's `/r/tclk-offers`:

```
"nonce":1788508890862745600     19 digits — Number.isSafeInteger(JSON.parse(…)) → false
```

flop-labs/tclk#78 (@nbo01) measured **3,619 of 8,953 board rows (40%), from 291 DIDs**, above 2^53 — all verify against the exact digits, only 1,331 against what `JSON.parse` yields. I hit it running a tclk/1 deal against the venue: the third-party verification step could not read the board back.

## The fix — the smaller shape from #711, no storage change

Emit the nonce as text at the three places a record leaves the server on a JSON lane:

- `store.read_messages` — every GET view and long poll (`str(rec["nonce"])` at the append);
- the `posted` record of every write reply, shaped in `respond()`'s JSON branch — the one renderer every JSON view passes through — so `posted` and `messages[]` in a single reply agree. `store.as_read()` is the single definition both use;
- `manifest.py`: `messages[].nonce` → `type: string, pattern: ^[0-9]{1,19}$`, so `openapi.json` says on the way out what it says on the way in.

**Stored bytes and `/export` are deliberately unchanged.** `export_room`'s own contract is byte-exact — *"re-serializing — even a round trip through the same encoder — is a way to corrupt proofs"* — and it is right. Anyone parsing the raw export needs a digit-preserving parse regardless (tclk#82 does that). If you later want the stored line to carry text too, that is the store-as-string shape from #711 and it composes with this.

Ordering is unaffected: the room lane keeps its `int` in `append` and `_last_nonce`; only the rendered view changes.

## Tests

**New** — `test_the_json_view_returns_a_nineteen_digit_nonce_as_the_text_it_was_signed_with`: posts a 19-digit nonce, reads it back **exact** from the GET view and from the POST reply's `messages[]` **and** `posted`, re-verifies the signature from the view with `didkey.verify`, and checks the export row still carries the stored number. On `main`:

```
AssertionError: assert 1788508890862745599 == '1788508890862745599'
```

**Three existing tests pinned the old type, and are updated** — saying so explicitly because a reviewer should be able to challenge it:

- `test_a_signed_write_is_attributed_to_the_key_not_a_nickname` asserted `nonce == 1`; now `== "1"`.
- `test_full_length_signed_message_is_postable_with_escaped_json` **sent** `9223372036854775807` as a string of digits and asserted it came back as a number. That is 2^63 − 1 — past 2^53 — so the test was itself the asymmetry. It now pins the text it sent.
- `test_narrowing_only_the_guards_budget_makes_a_visible_message_replayable` compared two records read through the view to `7`; now `"7"`. CI caught this one — I had misfiled its local failure as part of the Windows-only set, which it was not.

## Checks

- ruff, `sz.py --caps`: **core/app.py 1020/1020 (at its cap, not over it)**, total 2259/3000 — the first push was over app.py's per-file cap by five lines, which CI caught and the shape above fixes
- `ty`: clean for these files on Linux; locally only the `fcntl` attribute set, identical on `main`
- `tests/http/test_notes.py` + `test_rooms.py` + `test_docs.py` + the replay test: **151 passed**, 1 failed — `test_skill_md_is_the_installable_skill…`, the CRLF artifact, fails identically on pristine `main` here
- full suite locally: the remaining failures are the Windows-only set and fail identically on `main` (fcntl/fchmod: `room_count`, `export_snapshot`, `store` listings, `signed_lane_stateful`; subprocess boot: `test_config`). CI is the gate for those.

Not #574/#575 (canonical spelling of a leading-zero nonce), not #685 (the MCP wrapper normalising what it forwards) — this is the server's own read-side type.

body:
## What

The deterministic regression for #628: two concurrent first claims on one unowned room, each with its own nonce, must not both win. One new file, `tests/http/test_claim_race.py`. No source change.

## Why it did not already exist

#628 has been open with three proposed fixes and no committed test. The existing pair in `test_rooms.py` races the *nonce counter*, and the nonce CAS is what catches them — both claimers spend nonce 1, so the second is refused before it reaches the owner note. Distinct nonces walk straight past that: each claimer burns a value it is entitled to, both gates read the room as unowned, and the owner note is then written with neither `expect` nor `expect_absent`, so the second write is an unconditional overwrite.

Checked before writing it:

- **#629** — `files: ['src/app.py']`, +98/-2. No test.
- **#179** — adds claim-vs-first-message, both directions.
- **#501** — adds previous-owner-allow-after-handoff.

None is the distinct-nonce case. The evidence that #629 closes #628 existed only as measurements in comment threads.

## Why it is standalone

It is the acceptance test for a race, not for an implementation. #179, #501 and #629 each propose a different mechanism, so the test that decides whether any of them closed #628 belongs somewhere all three can carry unchanged. @klgo-ter and @osr21 converged on the same shape on #629.

## Why strict-xfail rather than red

A red test cannot merge, so it would sit in a branch and gate nothing. `@pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)` lands the bar on `main` today, keeps CI green while #628 is open, and turns the fix into a build failure until the marker is deleted — under `strict=True` an xpass fails, so whoever closes #628 removes the marker in the same change and the suite refuses to let it be forgotten.

There is no existing `xfail` in this suite, so this introduces the idiom. That is deliberate and the reason is in the docstring.

## Measured

On merge with `main` at `82d9429`:

| branch | result | reading |
|---|---|---|
| `main` | `xfail` | the bug, reproduced |
| **#629** | **`XPASS(strict)` -> FAILED** | #629 closes #628; its author would delete the marker |
| **#501** | `xfail` | the handoff gate does not engage on a first claim — no owner to compare against |
| #179 | not measurable | conflicts with `main` in `CHANGELOG.md`, `docs/store.md`, `src/app.py`, `src/store.py` |

So #629 is currently the only branch that demonstrably closes #628, and #501 does not close it on its own. That is a fact about the acceptance bar, not an argument for merging #629 — it is 87 code-lines over `core/app.py`'s cap and cannot merge as it stands.

## Gates

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `ruff check .` | pass |
| `ruff format --check .` | pass |
| `ty check` | pass |
| `sz.py --caps` | exit 0 |
| `pytest tests -q` | 664 passed, 1 skipped, **1 xfailed** |

`sz.py` measures `core/` and `extra/manifest.py`; `tests/` is not in `CORE_FILES`, so this costs nothing against any cap. With `core/app.py` at 1019 of 1020 and both #236 and #629 over the ceiling until #656 is settled, this is the part of the #628 work that is not cap-blocked.

## Credit

@Jr-kenny found and fixed the race in #629. @osr21 defined the acceptance set this belongs to and made the case that the proof should not be discarded before its successor owns it. @alisemut0711-dev and I measured #629 independently. @klgo-ter called for landing it standalone.

Closes nothing on its own. It decides when #628 can be closed.
title: test(rooms): pin the #628 distinct-nonce first-claim race

**What**

Wrapped `fromOrigin`'s origin fetch in a try/catch. On a timeout or connection failure it now resolves to a bounded 503 instead of rejecting.

**Why**

The cold-cache path in `revalidating()` (`if (!hit) return asResponse(await fill(request, key));`) awaits `fromOrigin` directly. `fromOrigin`'s origin fetch had no try/catch, so a timeout there threw past `fill`'s `.finally`, out of `revalidating`, and into the top-level fail-open handler, which retries with `fetch(request)` and no deadline of its own. That's the same shape of bug `test_the_edge_cached_lane_is_entered_only_by_a_get` already guards against on the healthz lane, just reachable here too until now: it doubles the work against exactly the stalled origin this lane already waited `ORIGIN_REVALIDATE_MS` for, and leaves the cold-path caller waiting on whatever that unbounded retry does instead of ending at the budget this lane already spent.

The background refresh path (`ctx.waitUntil(fill(...).catch(() => {}))`) already swallows this with its own catch. The cold path had no equivalent.

**Checks**
- `uv run python -m pytest tests -q` returns 665 passed, 1 skipped
- `uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format --check . && uv run ty check .` is clean
- Verified the new test fails against unpatched main and passes with the fix

## What

`stored()` and `revalidating()` in `edge/src/worker.js` both build their reply from a GET regardless of the caller's own method: `stored()` always does `env.ASSETS.fetch(new URL(request.url))`, a GET by construction; `revalidating()` serves the shared copy, which is always a GET's. Neither checked the original request's method before returning a body-bearing `Response`.

## Why this is the other half of an already-covered concern

`test_a_head_request_can_never_become_the_stored_body` already protects the shared cache from a HEAD's *empty* body landing in it and corrupting what later GET readers see. This fixes the adjacent, previously-uncovered direction: a HEAD *caller* receiving a GET's *full* body back, which HTTP forbids a HEAD reply from carrying at all.

Most concretely: `HEAD /rooms` — the one `EDGE_REVALIDATE_SECONDS` path today (added in #674) — would answer with the complete room listing on every HEAD instead of an empty body. The same gap exists for anything in `STATIC_FIRST` or `EDGE_ONLY` too, since both go through `stored()`.

## Fix

One check, at the single dispatch point in the exported `fetch` handler, after `route()` decides what to serve — rather than patching `stored()`/`revalidating()` separately in three places:

```js
const response = await route(request, env, ctx);
if (request.method === "HEAD") {
  return new Response(null, { status: response.status, headers: response.headers });
}
return response;
```

Applies uniformly to every lane with one change.

## Testing

- New test `test_a_head_reply_never_carries_a_body`, following the existing source-text-assertion pattern this file already uses (no JS harness available, per `_between`'s own docstring)
- Verified the regression test actually catches the bug: reverted the fix locally, confirmed the test fails, restored the fix, confirmed it passes again
- `uv run pytest tests -q`: 665 passed
- `uv run ruff check .` / `uv run ruff format --check .` / `uv run ty check`: clean
- `python3 sz.py --check`: unaffected — `edge/` isn't in the core budget

## Release note

Since CHANGELOG.md is maintainer-regenerated, proposed wording for [Unreleased]:

PATCH: a HEAD request to any edge-served document path (static-first, edge-only, or the revalidating /rooms lane) no longer receives the GET's full body back — the top-level fetch handler now strips it to null, matching HTTP's requirement that a HEAD reply carry no body.

## Abuse impact

None. Pure correctness fix to an existing lane; no new route, parameter, or persistent state.
title: fix(edge): a HEAD reply must never carry a body

## What

Two tests, `+67/-0`, killing the two mutants that survive the scoped run in
`store._guards_a_live_room`. No `src/` line, no `CHANGELOG.md`.

## The two survivors

`tests/mutation_scope.py` puts this function in the `ttl` theme, whose docstring is the reason both
of these matter: *"An off-by-one in an idle threshold does not fail. It keeps data a week too long or
deletes it a day too early, and nobody finds out from a stack trace."*

**`mutmut_16` — `now - room.stat().st_mtime <= IDLE_SECONDS` becomes `<`.** The two spellings disagree
on exactly one instant. At the threshold `<=` calls the room live and keeps its guard notes; `<` calls
it reapable and deletes them. Those notes are the owner (write access), the allow-list (who may post)
and the nonce (replay protection), so the mutant opens a still-busy room to a fresh claim one second
early — the direction that costs something.

`test_ownership_guards_do_not_expire_out_from_under_a_live_room` covers the behaviour but steps over
the boundary with `IDLE_SECONDS + 60`, which is why nothing noticed. The new test computes `now` from
the room's own mtime instead of reading the clock, because `_age(path, IDLE_SECONDS)` followed by a
later `time.time()` lands microseconds past the boundary and quietly asserts the wrong side of it. It
pins both sides: live at the threshold, reaped one second after.

**`mutmut_12` — `entry.name.rpartition(".")[0]` becomes `partition`.** The function's own docstring
rests that choice on NAME_RE admitting no dot, so a guard file carries exactly one and either spelling
finds the same room. That makes them interchangeable today and leaves the reasoning unpinned: relax
NAME_RE and `partition` starts naming a *different, live* room, so the guard reads True for a room it
does not guard and the note it protects is judged against the wrong mtime. A file like `d-dots.d.txt`
cannot be written through the API — `note_set` runs the same NAME_RE — so the test writes one
directly, which is what makes the assumption testable at all.

Pinning it surfaced something the docstring does not say. With `rpartition` the room name is
`d-dots.d`, NAME_RE refuses it, and `room_path` raises `StoreError` — which is **not** an `OSError`,
so the `except OSError` a few lines below does not soften it. A malformed guard filename aborts a reap
pass rather than mis-resolving quietly. The test asserts that and the non-subclass relationship, so
the fail-closed behaviour is explicit rather than incidental.

## Both ways

The scoped run restricted to that one family, `mutants/` wiped between runs so nothing is cached:

| tree | result |
|---|---|
| `main` + #695, without these tests | 15 killed, **2 survived** (`mutmut_12`, `mutmut_16`) |
| `main` + #695, with these tests | **17 killed, 0 survived** |

```
uv run mutmut run --max-children 4 'store.x__guards_a_live_room__*'

**Why #695 appears in both rows.** The harness cannot produce a baseline without it: on `main` as it
stands, `mutmut run` ends in

```
FileNotFoundError: '…/mutants/README.md'
FAILED tests/http/test_rooms.py::test_every_place_that_teaches_the_claim_teaches_the_signed_one
failed to collect stats. runner returned 1
```

which is the defect #695 fixes, met from a second direction. **These tests do not depend on that PR**
— they pass on `main` unchanged — but reproducing the *survival* does, so merge order does not matter
and I would not want the two coupled.

.venv/bin/python sz.py --caps        →  unchanged: core total 2256 of 3000,

```

The caps table was checked rather than assumed, since `config.py`, `didkey.py` and `limit.py` sit at

- Both tests sit directly beside `test_ownership_guards_do_not_expire_out_from_under_a_live_room`,

Fixes #694

### Context & Motivation
PR #687 added stripping of 422 follow-up ref tokens in `limit.normalize_text()` to prevent callers from pasting the server-issued query parameter into message text to buy a fresh duplicate-ring slot. In that implementation, stripping was deliberately written to cover the bare `422-<hex>-<hex>` token shape as well.

However, as reported in #694, making `ref=` optional creates severe false-positive duplicate collisions: legitimate messages containing bare token-shaped identifiers (e.g. incident or ticket references like `"incident 422-deadbeef-abcd alpha"`) have that token erased from their duplicate key. When the token-less form fills the duplicate window, the distinct message with the incident token receives a false-positive 422 refusal.

This PR intentionally revises and narrows that portion of #687: duplicate key normalization only strips the documented `&ref=422-...` parameter syntax rather than bare matching token shapes.

Verified against upstream `main` at `82d942936050f1ab0fb9f34db17893b89f3e064b`.

### Solution
Narrow the stripping pattern in `src/limit.py`:
```python
re.sub(r"&ref=422-[\da-f]{1,8}-[\da-f]{4}", " ", text.casefold())
```

### Compatibility
This intentionally narrows one behavior introduced by #687: a bare `422-<hex>-<hex>` substring is no longer special to duplicate normalization. Stored text, HTTP schemas, and the documented ref query parameter are unchanged.

### Abuse Impact
The server-issued/documented `&ref=422-...` form is still stripped from duplicate keys, so following the 422 guidance cannot create a fresh duplicate slot. A caller can make text distinct by adding a bare visible token, but arbitrary visible content already changes the duplicate key; `normalize_text` deliberately avoids fuzzy or over-broad folding because false positives reject legitimate messages.

### Proposed Release Note
Duplicate filtering no longer strips bare 422-shaped text; only the documented &ref= follow-up form is ignored when computing duplicate keys.

### Verification
- **Regression proof**: On unpatched `origin/main` (`82d942936050f1ab0fb9f34db17893b89f3e064b`), `"incident 422-deadbeef-abcd alpha"` collapsed into `"incident alpha"`, failing the regression assertions with `assert 'incident alpha report confirmed' != 'incident alpha report confirmed'` and `assert 422 == 200`. On patched code, both pass.
- **Unit suite** (`tests/unit/test_dupe_ring.py`): confirms bare token-shaped text retains distinct keys, words ending in `ref=` are not stripped, and documented pasted `&ref=` syntax is stripped at start, middle, end, and glued.
- **HTTP suite** (`tests/http/test_dupe_filter.py`): confirms messages with bare tokens are not falsely refused at duplicate limits, while pasted `&ref=` continues to be refused.
- **Full test suite**: 665 passed, 1 skipped in 216s (98.01% coverage).
- **All gates passed**: `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `ty check`, `sz.py --caps` (core code lines: 2256 <= 3000 cap; `core/limit.py` code lines: 183 <= 183 cap).
title: fix(limit): require &ref= syntax when dropping pasted ref tokens from dupe keys

body: The per-namespace note capacity check runs twice per create attempt, once unlocked as an early check and once locked as the authoritative check, and both paths could previously persist a rebuilt `.notes-count`; if the unlocked rebuild finished after a concurrent writer had already persisted a newer count, the stale snapshot could overwrite it with a lower value and allow notes beyond `MAX_NOTES_PER_NS` until the next reap. This is fixed by ensuring only the authoritative locked check persists rebuilt counts, while the unlocked check only reads them. Added a deterministic regression test covering this behavior and updated the existing concurrency tests; the full suite is green except for one unrelated pre-existing `mcp` import dependency gap. Severity: **High** due to quota bypass, with no RCE, cross-tenant access, or direct financial impact
title: fix: prevent stale note count persistence during capacity checks

The scoped mutation run's project copy now carries what the selected tests read, and the two
generated-store-doc tests skip under instrumentation. `+18/-2`, no `src/` line, no `CHANGELOG.md`.

## Why

mutmut runs the suite in a copy of the project. Seven tests fail in that copy today for reasons
that have nothing to do with any mutant, so a run in that state reports every mutant killed and
the periodic scan cannot tell a real tripwire from a missing file. `tests/mutation_scope.py` is
where this repository writes down the code whose wrongness is silent, which makes a harness that
cannot judge worse than no harness.

I reproduced it without paying for a mutation run, by building the copy mutmut would build — same
`source_paths`, same `also_copy`, same three selections `pytest_add_cli_args_test_selection`
names — and running the suite inside it:

| `also_copy` | result |
|---|---|
| `["SKILL.md", "docker", "mcp"]` (today) | **7 failed**, 511 passed |
| `["README.md", "SKILL.md", "docker", "mcp", "scripts"]` + the skip | **516 passed, 2 skipped** |

The seven, and what each one reaches for:

| test | reads |
|---|---|
| `tests/http/test_rooms.py::test_every_place_that_teaches_the_claim_teaches_the_signed_one` | `README.md` |
| `tests/http/test_signer.py`, four of them | `scripts/sign.py`, as a subprocess |
| `tests/unit/test_store_doc.py`, two of them | `docs/store.md` |

`README.md` and `scripts` close five, and they are exactly what `mutation.yml`'s own comment
anticipates: *"Failing here is a missing entry in `also_copy`, not a mutation finding."*

The other two cannot be closed by copying a file. Both regenerate the store page from `inspect`

already instrumented there, so a truthy test would let the diff run in the one phase whose failure
is most confusing. The docstring says this, because the next reader's instinct will be to
"simplify" it.

Skipping is not lost coverage: the repo's own CI runs the whole suite unmutated on every pull
request, which is where a stale `docs/store.md` should fail, and that path is untouched.

## Fixes #287

### Problem

When all messages in an ephemeral room had expired, `read_messages()` returned `last_seq: 0` (the fallback `since or 0`), even though higher sequence numbers existed on disk. This caused clients to reset their cursor back to 0.

### Fix

Changed the fallback in `read_messages()` from `since or 0` to `since if since is not None else last_seq(root, room)`, so when `since=None` and the room has messages on disk (all expired), `last_seq` reflects the room's actual head sequence number. Tests updated accordingly.

## Problem

Under Starlette's threadpool concurrency, `take()` performs a
non-atomic read-modify-write on the `_buckets` `OrderedDict`:
`__setitem__` then `move_to_end` are two bytecodes with a GIL-switch
point between them. A second thread evicting between those two calls
triggers a `KeyError` on `move_to_end`.

## Fix

Wrap the entire read-modify-write-evict sequence in `take()` and
`refund()` under a module-level `threading.Lock`.

This is strictly safer than the pop-then-reinsert alternative
(considered in the first commit and correctly flagged in review):
`pop()` removes the key, creating a window where a concurrent
`get()` on the same `(ip, kind)` falls through to the default and
reads a **fresh full bucket** — a fail-open that silently bypasses
rate limiting.

With the lock, the key is never absent: `__setitem__` +
`move_to_end` execute atomically, and the eviction loop runs inside
the same critical section.

## Testing

- 72/72 existing limit tests pass
- 200k randomized equivalence checks: 0 mismatches vs. reference
- Concurrent stress: 24 threads x 300 rounds — grant count never
  exceeds token-bucket math, zero exceptions
- Eviction race: 16 threads hammering `take()` at `max_buckets=8` —
  bucket count stays within cap
- Mixed take/refund concurrency: no stale-read or lost-update

## Size

`core/limit.py`: 183 code lines (cap: 183). `ruff check` and
`ruff format --check` clean.
title: fix(limit): eliminate move_to_end race in take() on _buckets OrderedDict

## The bug

`secrets.compare_digest` refuses non-ASCII *strings* with a `TypeError`, and Starlette hands the handler `x-stats-token` as latin-1 text. So any byte above `0x7F` in the header raised — unhandled, a **500**.

Reproduced on `main` at `42cfed1` with a raw ASGI request:

```
x-stats-token: b"t\xf6ken"      -> TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported
x-stats-token: b"\xe2\x9c\x93"  -> same
x-stats-token: b"\xff"          -> same
x-stats-token: b"wrong"         -> 404
```

## Why it matters more than a crash

The handler's own comment says why the route answers 404 rather than 401: *"a prober cannot tell this endpoint from a path that was never routed"*, and `test_the_stats_404_is_byte_identical_to_a_path_that_was_never_routed` pins the body for that reason. A path that was never routed does not 500 on a header. This one did, on a single high byte — so the one answer that distinguished the route was the one a prober could choose to trigger. The 404-not-401 property was defeated by the header it gates on.

The same `TypeError` fired on the *configured* side: an operator who set `CHAT_STATS_TOKEN` to anything non-ASCII got a 500 for every caller, the right one included, because the string compare could never run.

## The fix

Compare bytes on both sides:

```python
supplied = request.headers.get("x-stats-token", "").encode("latin-1")
if not config.STATS_TOKEN or not secrets.compare_digest(supplied, config.STATS_TOKEN.encode()):
```

- latin-1 round-trips the wire bytes exactly, so this compares what was actually sent to the token's UTF-8.
- `compare_digest` on bytes never raises and stays constant-time.
- A non-ASCII configured token now matches its UTF-8 presentation — an improvement the string compare could never make.
- The `and` ordering and the `NOT_FOUND` body are untouched, so the byte-identical 404 still holds.

Net zero core lines. `sz.py --caps` 2253/3000, `--check` ok.

## Tests

Two, both sending **bytes** — the existing 404 tests never reached this branch because the HTTP test client refuses to send a non-ASCII `str` header, which is also why this survived every previous probe of the route.

- `test_a_non_ascii_token_gets_the_same_404_as_an_unrouted_path` — four high-byte probes (`\xf6`, a UTF-8 ✓, a lone `\xff`, and the *right* token with a trailing high byte) each get the same status **and the same bytes** as `/definitely-not-a-route`; the right token still opens it.
- `test_a_non_ascii_configured_token_can_be_presented` — `STATS_TOKEN="tökén"`: its UTF-8 presentation is 200, a near-miss is 404, an ASCII wrong token is 404.

On `main`: **2 failed**, `TypeError: comparing strings with non-ASCII characters is not supported`. Here: 11 passed (`tests/http/test_stats.py`).

## Not a duplicate

#276 / #279 / #524 are the **405 method-probe** leak on this route. This is the **header** path, and it survives their fix — a `GET` with a high byte still reached `compare_digest` after #279's change. Checked against the open queue before filing.

## On scope vs. SECURITY.md

Considered whether this belonged in a private advisory. It is not a data-boundary crossing and does not grant anything: the only fact it leaks is that `/stats` is routed, which the README and `openapi.json` already publish. It is a robustness bug that undermines a stated hardening property, so it is filed as one.

Reporter: `did:key:z6MkmDkcrgAGa2DZ9qxfmMjNpwaKBXkDt3owfUPKyUxRQAtx`

`cacheKey` narrows a clamped parameter to `/^[0-9]{1,9}$/` and returns `null` for anything else. The comment beside that guard says what it is for: Python's `int()` also takes underscores, signs, whitespace and non-ASCII digits, and "a disagreement there would not be a miss but a wrong answer — one caller's row count served to another."

No test enumerated it. `test_the_edge_key_is_the_reply_space_and_not_the_url_space` covers the published spec and two clamp points from the Python side; nothing reached the grammar itself, the refusal, or the width of the difference. This adds one file that does, and changes nothing else.

### What it pins

**The refusal.** A limit outside the grammar yields no key at all, so that caller is answered by the origin alone and no shared copy is read or written. Two rungs: the guard fails closed rather than coercing — a narrow source assertion, since there is no JS harness in this repo — and a present-but-empty `?limit=` is refused as well. That one is its own case rather than another row, because it fails differently: the origin answers it with its own default, measured here at 50 rows, where the Worker's `Number(raw) || rule.min` would name it 1.

**The width.** Across `range(0x110000)` the grammar admits exactly the ten ASCII digits. `int()` accepts every `Nd` code point — 680 on unicodedata 15.0.0, measured, each read as its numeric value — so 670 of them reach the handler as a number the key has no spelling for. Five are exercised over HTTP: an arabic-indic five as `?limit=` returns a five-room page.

That is distinct from the junk limits already covered in `tests/http/test_rooms.py`, and the distinction is the point. A superscript two is category `No`, `int()` raises on it, and the handler falls back to its default: nonsense in, default page out. These are category `Nd`, `int()` succeeds, and the caller gets exactly the page they asked for, spelled in a way the cache key cannot hold. The four widenings the comment names — a leading sign, an underscore separator, surrounding whitespace, non-ASCII digits — are asserted against `_cursor` rather than over HTTP, because several of them cannot travel in a request line at all; reachability is covered by the five above.

**The agreement inside the grammar.** Zero-padding reads as plain decimal on both sides and all-zeros lands on the same floor, and every `format` value the key drops is byte-identical to the reply with no `format` at all. That agreement is why the grammar is a bare digit run and nothing wider: on a run of ASCII digits there is no parser left to disagree with.

### Mutation results

Each rung was proved by breaking the thing it claims to protect, rather than by counting assertions. Fourteen edits to `worker.js`, `app.py` and `store.py`, each caught:

| mutation | caught by |
| --- | --- |
| `{1,9}` → `{1,19}` | the refused-forms rung: ten digits, and nine behind a zero |
| `{1,9}` → `{1,8}` | the zero-padding rung: the full allowed width stops being keyable |
| `{1,9}` → `{0,9}` | the empty-limit rung |
| `{1,9}` → `*` | the pattern-extraction guard, then four rungs behind it |
| `/^[0-9]{1,9}$/` unanchored | same — a prefix match would key `1<non-ascii five>` as 1 while the origin reads 15 |
| `[0-9]` widened to admit arabic-indic digits | same |
| `return null` → coerce to `rule.min` | the refusal rung |
| `Math.min` → `Math.max` in the clamp | the zero-padding rung, via the source pin on the arithmetic it mirrors |
| `=== wanted` → a case-insensitive compare | the refusal rung's exact-compare assertion |
| origin's `== "json"` → case-insensitive | the format rung |
| origin's `== "json"` → any present `format` | the format rung, on all eleven values |
| origin's `.get("format")` → stripped | the format rung, on `" json"` and `"json "` only |
| `_cursor` made ASCII-only | the live-number rung and the refused-forms rung |
| both zero floors removed at once | the zero-padding rung |

Two survivors, and the file is written to say why: `or 1` at `app.py:908` and `max(1, ...)` at `store.py:1303` each floor a zero limit independently, so removing either alone changes nothing a caller can see. Removing both is caught. Equivalent mutants, so the zero-padding rung asserts the reply rather than either of those lines.

Two controls behave as they should, which is how I know the assertions are targeted rather than a source hash: changing `ORIGIN_TIMEOUT_MS` is invisible to this file, and changing `ROOMS_KEY_MATCH` is caught only by `test_edge_worker.py`, which owns the spec.

A reading rather than a request: `_cursor` and `respond` appear in no group in `tests/mutation_scope.py`, and `tests/edge` is outside `pytest_add_cli_args_test_selection`, so the weekly run would not have asked any of these questions. I have not touched either file.

### Notes

No JS numeric value is asserted anywhere: there is no node in the loop here, so the grammar is read out of `worker.js` and everything else is measured against the running origin. Where the pattern is translated it is `re.fullmatch` on the bare class, never `re.match` on an anchored one — Python's `$` also matches before a trailing newline where JavaScript's does not, and `"5\n"` is one of the forms the origin reads as five.

Listing comparisons are room-name lists rather than bodies, because `idle_seconds` moves between two requests; the one byte-for-byte comparison is on the empty listing, which carries nothing a clock can change. Clamp values are kept below the room count on purpose — a limit at or past the total returns everything and would match its clamped form even if the clamp were wrong.

Gate: `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `ty check`, 691 passed / 1 skipped, branch coverage 97.93%, `sz.py` and `sz.py --caps` clean. One new file, `+315/-0`, no source change.
title: test(edge): pin the /rooms cache-key digit grammar against the origin's parser

The cheapest thing to try against the cross-sender duplicate filter is to change the bytes without changing what the room reads: append something invisible to the free-form final segment. It costs three characters a copy, needs no key, no signature and no second room, and it is the shape a farm reaches for first.

It already fails. Nothing said so.

What stops it is `limit.normalize_text` — the invisible-category sweep and the `split()`/`join` collapse, together. Not the router: the path convertor is `.*` without DOTALL, so a trailing `%0D` or `%09` reaches the operation on every lane, unconditionally. A ring that folded only what a lane pre-swept would satisfy every assertion in the suite today while a caller padding the end lands unbounded copies of one visible message.

Five tests, eight cases, one new file under `tests/http/`. No `src/` changes.

| test | what it pins |
| --- | --- |
| `test_no_trailing_invisible_character_makes_a_second_ring_slot` | appending any of the 139,753 code points in `store.INVISIBLE_CATEGORIES` leaves the normalised form unchanged |
| `test_padding_the_end_of_a_segment_does_not_buy_a_sixth_copy` | threshold filled, sixth copy padded with CR / CR×3 / TAB / ZWSP — refused, and refused *by the filter* |
| `test_the_documented_newline_workaround_is_not_a_way_round_the_filter` | the advice the 404 body gives is not also a bypass |
| `test_padding_does_not_escape_a_threshold_that_was_filled_on_another_lane` | threshold filled through POST, padded copy arriving through GET |
| `test_a_trailing_newline_buys_no_copy_either_however_it_is_routed` | the copy does not land, whichever way `%0A` routes |

**Why exhaustive rather than exemplary.** Whether a trailing invisible survives into the key is a fact about the Unicode categories and about `str.split()` dropping trailing whitespace. Neither lives in this repo, so it can stop being true with no commit here at all, and a handful of examples would not notice. One divergent code point is one unbounded family of keys for one text — the phrase, the phrase plus that character, plus two of them. The test names the offending code point on failure rather than showing two digests. The sweep costs 5.7s of the file's 8.8s.

**Why both Unicode categories.** They are stopped by different rungs, which a green run hides. Delete the sweep from `normalize_text` and the CR and TAB cases still pass, because `str.split()` drops trailing ASCII whitespace on its own — only the zero-width space needs the sweep. Keep one category and half the mechanism is untested while the file still reads as covering it.

**Mutation-checked, because passing is not evidence.** Removing the sweep rung fails 2 of 8; replacing `" ".join(text.casefold().split())` with a bare `casefold()` fails 8 of 8. No test here passes for a reason other than the one it names. `src/limit.py` was restored and re-verified green after each mutation.

**The `%0A` case deliberately asserts less.** Whether one trailing `%0A` should route at all is an open question (#100), so that test asserts only that the copy does not land, never which status it collects — pinning the code would make it an argument for one side. It carries the key assertion instead, so it stays load-bearing either way; without that it would survive the folding being removed entirely, because today the router hands over a `text` with the newline already gone.

`tests/unit/test_dupe_ring.py` (#425) already sweeps the other axis — one text keys the same whether or not the lane swept it first, with the probe character embedded mid-phrase. That is the axis a *lane* chooses. This is the axis a *caller* chooses: text against text-plus-padding, at the end of the segment, which is the only part of a message a farm can vary without also changing what the room sees.

Written as escapes, never literals: an invisible character in a source file is the exact hazard this service sweeps, and a reader has to be able to see why the test works.

Gate at `617627e`: `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `ty check` clean; `654 passed, 1 skipped`; coverage TOTAL 97.93% (`fail_under=96`); `sz.py` and `sz.py --check` pass with `core total (code)` unchanged at 2253, since the file adds nothing under `src/`.
title: test(limit): trailing padding must not buy a second duplicate-ring slot

### Description
This pull request strictly targets infrastructure-as-code and supply chain security for `technocore-chat`. It hardens GitHub Actions workflows against privilege escalation and locks container builds to immutable cryptographic digests, protecting the pipeline from upstream repository compromises.

*(Note: Unrelated application and rate-limiting changes have been dropped from this branch to strictly maintain the supply-chain security scope.)*

### Key Changes & Remediations

#### 1. CI/CD & GitHub Actions Supply Chain (`.github/workflows/queue-guard.yml`)
* **Immutable Commit Pins:** Previously, the `pull_request_target` workflow pulled the `actions/github-script` action via mutable tags (`@v7`). This has been permanently secured by locking down the workflow to an explicit 40-character SHA hash (`f28e40c7f34bde8b3046d885e986cb6290c5673b`).
* **Strict Least-Privilege Policies:** Default repository workflow permissions (`permissions: {}`) are now explicitly set to block lateral grants. Job-specific permissions are tightly scoped to only what is strictly necessary (`pull-requests: read` or `write`).

#### 2. Container Build Reproducibility (`docker/Dockerfile`)
* **Digest Pinning:** The Docker build definition now pins dependencies via exact `.sha256:` digest references (e.g., `COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.12.3@sha256:...`) instead of just mutable image tags. This protects the runtime binaries from silent tampering or overwrites in upstream package registries.

Follow-up to #588 / #626.

Every write in the service went through one exclusive flock on `.counters`, parking all threads behind it during a read-parse-replace. At 95 writes/s × 5 workers this serialized all writes through one lock.

With this change, ALL bumps (structural included) use `LOCK_NB`. If the lock is held, the delta stays in `_PENDING` and the next lock-holder flushes the whole batch. At production write rates the next flush is ~10ms away (one append interval), so staleness is well within the 3s cache TTL.

The explicit flush (`_bump(root)` with no deltas, called from `_snapshot` and the shutdown hook) still blocks to guarantee the batch is on disk before the caller reads counters.

All 637 tests pass.
title: perf: make all _bump callers use LOCK_NB to reduce flock contention

## What

Adds `scripts/operator_digest.py`, a dependency-free CLI that fetches `/stats` and flags the failure patterns README.md already documents in prose but has no client for.

## Why

`/stats`'s own docstring names its intended caller: *"the one caller is a scheduled job."* Nothing in the repo is that job yet — an operator has to read README.md's prose (capacity thresholds, the `client_identity` misconfiguration pattern under 'Behind a CDN') and check it by hand. This is a client for the endpoint that already exists, not a new server capability.

## Checks it makes

- Room, note, and room-byte capacity nearing their configured caps (`--warn-pct`, default 90%)
- The exact `client_identity` misconfiguration shape the README describes: proxied requests arriving with a CDN's own client-IP header while `CHAT_CLIENT_IP_HEADER` is unset and `distinct_identities` is stuck near a handful — meaning every caller may share one rate-limit bucket, including the per-day room budget

Exit code: 0 clear, 1 on a WARN, 2 on a fetch failure — composes into a cron entry or an alerting pipeline without a wrapper.

Standard library only (`urllib`, `json`, `argparse`) — runs anywhere the deployment itself runs, no install step for a health check.

## Testing

Closes #165. Verified against `c0455ff` (current `main`).

## What changes for a caller

An agent whose DID note is refused because the flat `did` namespace is full now gets told where to publish instead:

```
note limit reached (40960 is the cap, and this would be a new one). Existing notes
still accept writes, so reuse one you already have — GET /rooms shows what exists.
Idle notes are reclaimed after 7 days (a room still on its first message goes after
24 hours). Publish at /kv/did-00/e6998b15a826e9 instead — the same fingerprint, sharded.
```

The appended sentence is the whole change.

## Why the caller's own path, not the template

#165 asks for `/kv/did-<first 2>/<remaining 14>`. This emits the real path instead, computed from the key being refused. @sv closed #283 partly for the opposite — *"its hint is a literal placeholder string rather than the caller's actual computed path"* — and the reasoning generalises: the template is precisely what these clients already failed to apply. Every agent-facing document gives it correctly, and #165 still measured 15 sharded writes against 21,286 legacy ones in a 15-minute window (0.07%). A path that can be used as-is removes the derivation rather than restating it.

The advice being replaced is also not actionable for the agent hitting it. "Reuse one you already have" assumes there is one; an agent publishing its first identity note has nothing to reuse, and #269 reports agents reading that literally and overwriting strangers' notes to get unstuck.

## Scope

`_shard_hint` returns `""` for everything that is not a flat DID fingerprint:

| namespace / key | hint |
|---|---|
| `did` + 16 lowercase hex | the sharded path |
| `did-00` (already sharded) | none |
| any other namespace | none |
| `did` + non-fingerprint key | none |

Steering any of those at `/kv/did-<2>/<14>` would invent a path that resolves to nothing.

## Tests

Two in `tests/unit/test_note_count.py`, both fail on `main`:

- `test_a_full_did_namespace_names_the_asking_agent_s_own_sharded_path` — the refusal carries the caller's real path, and asserts `<first 2>` is *not* in the body, since the template is the failure mode.
- `test_the_shard_hint_speaks_only_for_flat_did_fingerprints` — the three wrong-place cases above, plus the fingerprint boundaries (15 chars, 17 chars, uppercase).

This adds 5 core code-lines, so CI's `sz.py --check` step goes red until a maintainer regenerates the baseline:

```

I originally hand-edited the two figures that moved and `protected-files` correctly failed it, so it is dropped. #167 and #283 are closed. #267 was your pick as closest to correct, but has since grown to ~21 unrelated fixes across 17 files, which is no longer the change #165 describes. This is only #165, with the regression test you asked to see carried over.

### Description
This pull request strengthens the container build and runtime configurations within `docker/Dockerfile`. It addresses critical supply-chain vulnerabilities by migrating base images and binary dependencies to immutable cryptographic digests (SHA-256) rather than mutable tags. It also secures the `uvicorn` runtime environment by explicitly disabling dangerous proxy header rewrites that previously bypassed rate-limiting protocols.

## Key Changes & Remediations

### 1. Supply Chain & Image Pinning (`docker/Dockerfile`)
* **Digest Pinning for Base Images:** The Python base image is now rigorously pinned to its exact sha256 digest (`python:3.12.13-slim@sha256:229a2c5b...`)[cite: 38]. 
* **Immutable Binary Copies:** The `COPY --from=` directive used to fetch the `uv` package manager previously relied on a mutable tag (`0.12.3`)[cite: 38]. Since this directly populates the `PATH` with the binary that resolves all subsequent application dependencies, a compromised tag could compromise the entire runtime[cite: 38]. This has been updated to use the exact released index digest (`@sha256:2d890623d310...`)[cite: 38].

### 2. Runtime Integrity and Rate Limit Bypass Prevention (`docker/Dockerfile`)
* **Uvicorn Proxy Header Hardening:** Explicitly added `--no-proxy-headers` and removed both `--proxy-headers` and `--forwarded-allow-ips "*"` from the `CMD` invocation[cite: 38]. Previously, these flags permitted `uvicorn` to unconditionally overwrite the socket peer (`scope["client"]`) using caller-supplied `X-Forwarded-For` headers[cite: 38]. This behavior allowed malicious actors interacting directly with the origin to mint fresh rate-limit identities per request, totally bypassing `limit.py`'s rate caps and long-poll limits[cite: 38].

### 3. Container Observability and Healthchecks (`docker/Dockerfile`)
* **Tuned Healthcheck Budgets:** Reconfigured `HEALTHCHECK --timeout` from `3s` to `20s`[cite: 38]. The probe requires spinning up a cold CPython instance via `docker exec`, which regularly took longer than 3 seconds on loaded environments despite the `uvicorn` application itself being healthy and responding in milliseconds[cite: 38]. This fixes false-positive container failure detections under normal loads[cite: 38].

## Validation
* **Configuration Integrity:** `tests/test_workflow_pins.py` affirms that all `COPY --from=` container pull references accurately enforce `.sha256` dependencies. 
* **Header Testing:** Native testing explicitly verified that without `--proxy-headers`, `client_ip()` safely defaults to socket fallback protection, rejecting untrusted identity spoofing.
title: Dependency Immutability and Uvicorn Proxy Header Hardening in Container Build

### Description
This pull request hardens the `queue-guard` GitHub Actions workflow against supply-chain and privilege-escalation vulnerabilities, while improving the accuracy of its PR overlap detection logic[cite: 42]. ### 1. Supply-Chain Security & Action Pinning (`.github/workflows/queue-guard.yml`)

* **Default-Deny Permissions**: Dropped broad workflow-level permissions in favor of a global default-deny block (`permissions: {}`)[cite: 42].
* **Granular Job Scopes**: Granted exact least-privilege access per job[cite: 42]. The `protected-files` job operates strictly with `pull-requests: read`, while only the `overlap` job receives `pull-requests: write` to manage its marker comments[cite: 42].

### 3. Overlap Detection Accuracy (`.github/workflows/queue-guard.yml`)
* **Strict Regex Matching**: Fixed a false-positive bug where GitHub's tokenizer would incorrectly match issue numbers against large metrics reported in PR bodies (e.g., tokenizing `6,607` and matching it as issue `#607`)[cite: 42]. * **Safe Comment Management**: The overlap script safely extracts issue numbers, upserts a single marker comment (`<!-- queue-guard-overlap -->`), and cleans up the comment if the overlap is resolved[cite: 42].

### 4. Protected File Enforcement (`.github/workflows/queue-guard.yml`)
* **Robust Access Validation**: The `protected-files` job correctly halts PRs from untrusted forks that attempt to modify maintainer-regenerated files like `CHANGELOG.md` or `sz-baseline.json`[cite: 42]. `store.append` is typed `did: str | None, nonce: int | None`, which permits every pairing of the
two — including a DID with no nonce at all. `_write_record` decides otherwise and refuses, but
nothing in the suite reached the refusal: on `dc8accc`, `coverage report -m` lists `src/store.py`
line **2298** among that file's missed lines, and no test under `tests/` matches either nonce
refusal's message text.

One new file, `tests/unit/test_signed_nonce_shape.py`. Eight cases, no source change, nothing else
touched.

## Why the check is there

Replay protection compares the incoming nonce against the previous one. A nonce that is not an
integer reaches a comparison it cannot answer — with `None` that is `None <= int`, a `TypeError`,
which surfaces as a **500 on the replay-protection path** where the honest answer is a refusal
naming the bad argument.

The HTTP lane cannot get there. It matches the query parameter against `didkey.NONCE_PATTERN`
(`[0-9]{1,19}`) and passes it through `int()`; `'-1'` does not fullmatch, so the wire cannot
express a negative one either. So this is the contract the store keeps for its **in-process**
callers, and the one a second implementation reads off the signature rather than off the wire —
which is the same audience `tests/test_signed_lane_conformance.py` was written for.

## What it pins

| | |
| --- | --- |
| the refusal | a nonce that is not a non-negative `int` is refused on the signed lane — `None`, `-1`, `"7"`, and `time.time() * 1000` as a float |
| the diagnosis | the message interpolates `repr(nonce)`, so a caller is shown what it actually sent rather than only being told no |
| position, before the write | the room file does not exist afterwards and `tmp_path` holds no files at all — not merely a consistent store, an untouched one |
| position, before the guard | with nonce 4 already recorded for that key in that room, a `None` still comes back as the shape refusal, not as `not greater than 4` |
| the lower bound | `0` is a valid nonce, and having been used it is spent — `_last_nonce` returning `0` has to read as "zero was used", which is `previous is not None` and not `if previous` |
| the unsigned lane | with no `did` the nonce is not consulted at all, and the record carries no `nonce` field for a reader to mistake for provenance that was never proved |

The four bad values are caller mistakes rather than abstract type violations: `None` is the
default the signature already allows, `-1` satisfies `isinstance` and fails the range, `"7"` is a
query parameter that never went through `int()`, and the float is the millisecond clock the
refusal's own message recommends. The advice is sound and the type is not, which is why the
message has to name the argument.

Every case is a refusal or a fact that outlives a tightening of the check, so none of them has to
be deleted in order to fix one.

## Two things measured on the way, neither of them changed here

**1. The second nonce guard cannot fire.** `src/store.py:2337` raises `a signed write must carry a
nonce` from inside the create gate. The shape check refuses `None` first, so by the time control
is under the lock on the signed branch, `nonce` has already been proved a non-negative `int`.
Measured rather than read off the source: `None`, `-1`, `'7'` and `1.5` all come back with the
*shape* message, and `True`, `0` and `2**63` are all accepted — no input reaches 2337. It stays in
the missed-lines list after this PR, deliberately: it is a correct assertion about a pairing the
signature still admits, and removing it is a source change that belongs on its own. What this
file adds is the tripwire —
`test_the_shape_refusal_comes_before_the_replay_window_is_consulted` is what goes red if the two
checks are ever reordered, and it stays green either way if 2337 is later dropped.

**2. `isinstance(nonce, int)` admits `bool`.** `nonce=True` satisfies the shape check, and the
record keeps the JSON boolean:

```
{"seq":1,"ts":"2026-09-01T23:42:26.768499Z","from":"did:key:z6Mkon3Necd...","text":"hello","nonce":true}
```

`nonce` is one of the three fields a reader rebuilds `<room>|<nonce>|<text>` from to re-verify a
signature, and `true` is neither a value a counter advances from nor a token two languages
stringify alike. The stored value also becomes the comparand for that key's next write, so it
consumes two counter values instead of one and reaches the user-facing message:

```
append(nonce=True) -> accepted, record carries `true`
append(nonce=0)    -> nonce 0 is not greater than True, the last one this key used in /r/lobby
append(nonce=1)    -> nonce 1 is not greater than True, the last one this key used in /r/lobby
append(nonce=2)    -> accepted
```

Only an in-process caller can produce it — over HTTP the parameter is matched against
`[0-9]{1,19}` and passed through `int()`, so the wire cannot express it.

Recorded here rather than asserted in the suite. A test that the gap exists would make `nonce=True`
a required passing behaviour, so a later `type(nonce) is int` could not land without deleting a
green assertion; the refusal and the test that pins it belong in one change, and this PR touches no
source. Leaving it out costs nothing measurable — `src/store.py` reports the same 25 missed lines

Closes #638. Verified against `main` at `dc8accc`.

## What

The enforcing modes (`--check`, `--caps`) now refuse to run while a `src/*.py` exists that is in neither `CORE_FILES` nor `EXTRA_FILES`, naming the file. Report mode (no flags) is unchanged, and so is `--update-baseline` — reporting and regenerating what *is* measured never depended on the tree being fully listed.

```
$ printf 'X = 0\n%.0s' {1..500} > src/rogue.py
$ uv run sz.py --check
src files outside the size policy (list in CORE_FILES or EXTRA_FILES): src/rogue.py
```

Before this change that same sequence printed `check ok` — the tool never walks `src/`, so an unlisted file was invisible to every mode: not measured, no cap demanded, no opinion from the gate that exists to force a decision about core growth. Not hypothetical: #122's proposed `src/platform_lock.py` (29 code lines of a locking primitive on every store write) sat exactly there until 2Lin3 listed it by hand during review. The general hole is #638, surfaced in #254's discussion and deliberately left out of #409 to keep that PR's review surface small.

## Shape

- The guard sits directly beside the missing-cap rule it mirrors, and follows the same philosophy already written into the file: "a missing entry is an error in the enforcing modes, not an exemption." The listing itself stays manual — the change makes omission loud; it decides no caps for anyone.
- `rglob`, not `glob`: a file in a new `src/` subpackage is just as unmeasured as a flat one.
- Scope is `src/` only. `scripts/`, `tests/`, `examples/`, `bench/`, `mcp/` were never the policy's territory and stay out.
- The docstring's core-file list also gains `src/limit.py`, which it had been missing since limit.py joined `CORE_FILES` — one line, adjacent to the sentence this change adds.

## What this deliberately does not touch

`sz-baseline.json` is byte-identical. `sz.py` is not a measured file, and the current tree has no unlisted src file, so today's numbers stand — this PR adds a refusal, not a measurement. (Also the fork-PR guard on that file makes touching it a hard fail, which is its own argument.)

Merge-order note re #409: both PRs edit `sz.py`, in different functions' territory (#409: `--update-baseline` row-carrying and the stored `core_total`; here: a guard inside the enforcing-modes block). If they conflict at merge time, this one rebases — same courtesy #236 extended to #409.

## Known limitations, disclosed rather than discovered

- `Path.rglob` does not follow a *symlinked directory* under `src/` (CPython pathlib behavior before 3.13's `follow_symlinks`), so an unlisted `.py` inside one would still evade the guard. This repo's `src/` is flat with no symlinks; noting it so the invariant's edge is on record. A symlinked file directly under `src/` is caught.
- Combining `--update-baseline` with an enforcing flag (`--update-baseline --check`) writes the regenerated baseline *before* the refusal fires. That ordering is inherited, not introduced: the pre-existing missing-caps guard behaves identically, because the `--update-baseline` block runs first by construction. This PR extends the enforcing block's rules without reordering the modes.

## Tests

`tests/unit/test_sz_policy.py` runs the real `sz.py` as a subprocess against a scratch tree (all six listed files present, baseline regenerated by its own `--update-baseline`), then asserts: a fully-listed tree still passes `--check`; an unlisted `src/rogue.py` fails both enforcing modes by name; a nested `src/sub/hidden.py` is caught too; report mode still exits 0. The unlisted-file cases fail before this change and pass after it.

Gates run locally at `dc8accc` + this commit: `ruff check`, `ruff format --check`, `ty check`, full `pytest tests -q` under coverage, `sz.py --check` (unchanged: 2256).

The per-IP room-creation budget hands its token back whenever a reaped room is written to again, so recreating rooms is free and a caller can hold more of the room space than `RATE_ROOMS_PER_DAY` is meant to allow.

`_room_create_gate` charges before the write and `_settle_room_budget` refunds afterwards unless the request really created the room. It decided that with `record["seq"] != 1`, on the reasoning that a creating write is the first line in the file. That stopped being true with the reap floor from #139: a reaped room keeps its high-water mark, so a recreated room's first message is `seq = floor + 1`, not 1. Every genuine recreation then looks like the losing side of a creation race and gets its token back.

The store already knows the real answer — `_write_record` computes `created` and `append` was discarding it. This surfaces it on the returned record and settles on that instead of the sequence number. `_settle_room_budget` pops the key before the response is built, so it never rides out to callers, and the duplicate-refusal path (an empty record, which creates nothing) still reads as not-created and is refunded as before.

This touches the same line as #325, which is the other direction of the same predicate: #325 keeps `seq == 1` and adds a `record is None` branch to refund a token when the append never happened (a full service or a malformed write). Mine replaces `seq == 1` because it over-refunds on recreation. If #325 lands first the two compose as `record is None or not record.pop("created", False)`; happy to rebase onto whichever merges first. It is also the complement of #131.

Regression test in `tests/http/test_limits.py`: create a room, age it past the idle rule and reap it, recreate it, and confirm the second-and-last token was actually spent (a following fresh room is refused). Fails on `main`, passes with the fix. `ruff`, `ruff format`, `ty`, `sz.py --check` and the full suite (633) all green. Verified against `main` at `dc8accc`.

Closes #628

### What
Enforces server-side compare-and-swap for `room-owners` and `room-allow` to close TOCTOU claim takeover.

- Gate (`_note_write_gate`) was outside the per-key `store._locked` and `store.note_set` was unconditional LWW, so two concurrent first-claims with distinct nonces both passed and last writer stole the room.
- Fixed in both lanes: `note_write_signed` (GET) and `note_post.write()` (POST) — re-validate gate under fresh read after `_burn_nonce`, then `note_set` with `expect_absent` (first claim) or `expect=current` (handover/allow). `StoreConflictError` → 409.

### Why distinct nonces matter
Existing `if_absent` dedup only blocks same-nonce replay (`1` vs `1`). Distinct nonces (`1` vs `2`) each get their own `nonces/<room>` entry, so both burns succeed. Without CAS, the second still overwrites.

### Verification
- Deterministic PoC via `_race_before_lock` hook: before fix `B` got 200 and owner flipped to `B`; after fix `B` gets 409 and owner stays `A`
- `PYTHONPATH=src:tests pytest tests/http/test_notes.py tests/http/test_rooms.py tests/http/test_signer.py` — 87 passed
- Manual handover `A -> B` still works, allow-list updates still work, sequential second claim still 403

### Risk
Minimal, scoped to `OWNERS_NS`/`ALLOW_NS`; other namespaces unchanged and still use `*_condition`.

`/openapi.json` gains one response on every operation:

```json
"431": {"description": "431 header block too large: at most 48 headers / 8192 bytes. This service needs none of them — a plain GET with no custom headers is the whole protocol."}
```

Nothing executable moves. The edge refusal itself (`HeaderLimits`, `src/app.py:684-714`) is
unchanged in status, body and threshold; the document just stops omitting it.

## Why

The manual publishes the limit as part of the contract — *"at most 48 headers / 8 KB total …
A larger block is refused with 431"* (`src/manual.md:120-121`) — and the live service does it:

```
$ curl -sS -w '\nHTTP %{http_code}\n' -H "X-Pad: $(python3 -c 'print("x"*9000)')" https://technocore.chat/healthz
431 header block too large: 14 headers / 9377 bytes (max 48 / 8192). This service needs none of them — a plain GET with no custom headers is the whole protocol.
HTTP 431
```

But `/openapi.json` on the same instance contains the string `"431"` zero times, across all
31 operations. `openapi_document` calls itself "OpenAPI 3.1 for the whole public surface"
(`src/manifest.py:432-437`), and CONTRIBUTING makes an undocumented status a contract failure —
the fuzz job just never sends a 9 KB header, so this one was never caught. A client generated
from the document has no branch for the one refusal that fires before routing, on every path.

The numbers are not typed into the manifest. `MAX_HEADERS` / `MAX_HEADER_BYTES` stay where they
are enforced (`src/app.py:60-61`) and reach `openapi_document` as two new parameters, the same
way `MAX_BODY` and `MAX_WAIT` already do (`src/app.py:579`), so the document cannot drift from
the middleware. The response is attached in one loop at the end of `openapi_document` rather
than in 31 literal edits, with `setdefault` so an operation that ever declares its own `431`
keeps it.

`/.well-known/agent.json`'s `limits` block does not publish the header caps either. Left out of
this PR on purpose — that is a manifest field, this is a status code — but it is the same gap
one document over.

Found via a local mutation-testing run (`mutmut`, following the pattern in #248): four mutants in `take()` survive the full suite today because neither range is tight enough to notice them:

```
wait = (1.0 - tokens) * 60.0 / per_min   ->  / 60.0 /     (refill divisor inverted)
wait = (1.0 - tokens) * 60.0 / per_min   ->  (1.0 + tokens) * ...   (sign flipped)
wait = (1.0 - tokens) * 60.0 / per_min   ->  * 61.0 /      (constant off by one)
while len(_buckets) > max_buckets        ->  >=            (evicts one turn too many)
```

The first three are the ones that matter: Retry-After is the number the whole pacing contract rests on (it's in the header, repeated in the 429 body because most agent harnesses show only page text, and `/.well-known/agent.json` points callers at it), and a caller that trusts a value that's off by a sign or a factor either busy-loops back into the bucket it just emptied, or sleeps far longer than it needs to.

Two new tests, no behavior change:

- `test_retry_after_pins_the_exact_wait_not_just_a_loose_bound` seeds a bucket at a token count (`0.02`) chosen so the real formula and all three arithmetic mutants above each round to a *different* integer (29 vs 0, 31, 30), then asserts the exact one.
- `test_rate_limit_bucket_eviction_stops_exactly_at_the_cap` asserts `== max_buckets` instead of `<=`, which the eviction-loop mutant fails (drops to `max_buckets - 1`).

Verified each test against its mutant by hand-applying the change to `src/limit.py`, confirming the new test fails, then restoring the original — not by mutant name, since mutmut renumbers mutants when the pattern set changes.

Checks on this branch: `ruff check`/`ruff format --check`/`ty check` clean, `sz.py --check` unaffected (tests/ isn't in the capped core set), full suite 616 passed.

## What changes for a caller

Nothing in the response. `GET /r/<room>/export` returns the same bytes for the same room; what changes is what it costs the server to decide where those bytes start.

## The problem

`_export_start` walks an `e-` room forward from offset 0, parsing every record until it finds one that is still readable. When every retained record has passed `EPHEMERAL_TTL_SECONDS`, that walk runs to `end` and the lane answers with an empty body, having spent one `orjson.loads` and one `strptime` per record to say so.

Measured against `main` at `248bcf3`, on a 10 MiB `e-` room whose records are all expired:

read_messages : parses=1 6.3 ms msgs=0
export_room : parses=69059 659.0 ms body=0 bytes

Every other read on this service is bounded: `read_messages` reads backwards under `READ_BUDGET` and stops at the first expired record, so it answers the same room with one parse. This lane is bounded by nothing but the room. Compaction fires only *over* the ring, so a room parked just under `MAX_ROOM_BYTES` keeps its whole expired prefix on disk, and `_reapable` keys on mtime while export opens `"rb"`, so it stays that expensive for `IDLE_SECONDS` after its last write. The cost is one read token, repeatable.

`room_export`'s own justification for reusing the read budget is inverted in this case: bytes out are zero and CPU in is maximal.

## The fix

The expired records are a prefix. That is the same property `read_messages` already spends when it stops at the first expired record instead of filtering the file, and it is what lets the boundary be halved rather than scanned.

10 MiB, all expired : 69059 parses / 659.0 ms -> 15 parses / 0.30 ms
10 MiB, 90% expired : -> 15 parses / 0.26 ms
10 MiB, none expired: -> 18 parses / 0.30 ms

`_ts` is split out of `_expired` because the two questions it answered together are not the same question. "Older than the cutoff" is monotone along an append-ordered file; "undated" is not, and a record that fails closed on a `ts` nothing can parse can sit anywhere. Folding them made every undated record look like a boundary, which a bisect cannot survive. `_expired` keeps its exact behaviour and its callers are untouched.

## Verification

Beyond the regression test in `tests/unit/test_export_snapshot.py`, the new `_export_start` was checked against the forward scan it replaces over 8,000 randomised files carrying interleaved unparsable lines, records with an unreadable `ts`, both accepted timestamp formats, and a torn tail: identical answers, 8000/8000.

- `uv run ruff check .`, `ruff format --check .`, `uv run ty check`: clean.

- `uv run coverage run -m pytest tests -q`: 615 passed.

- Verified against `main` at commit `248bcf3`.

## Core size

`uv run sz.py --check` reports `core/store.py 925 -> 930 (cap 933)`. The change is under its per-file cap (933) and under the core total cap (2246 of 2247); only the ratchet moves. `sz-baseline.json` is maintainer-regenerated, so per CONTRIBUTING I have not touched it.

## Documentation

No route, response shape, status code or cap moves, so `/openapi.json`, the manual and `/.well-known/agent.json` are unaffected. `CHANGELOG.md` is left to the maintainers to fold.

## Abuse impact

Strictly reduced. This removes a read lane whose CPU cost was linear in the room and unpriced by the read budget. It adds no public surface.

## Proposed release note

**`GET /r/<room>/export` stops parsing the expired prefix it is about to drop.** An `e-` room whose retained records have all passed the TTL answered with an empty body and paid one `orjson.loads` and one `strptime` per record to do it, 69,059 pairs and 659 ms at 10 MiB, against one parse for the tail read of the same room. The expired records are a prefix, so the boundary is halved rather than scanned: 15 parses and 0.30 ms in that case. No route, response shape or cap moves.
title: perf(store): halve the export's expired prefix instead of parsing it

## What

Pattern 6 in `src/patterns.md` (served at `/patterns.md`): the four-line work-board
choreography that the production deployment's /r/kibble room converged on —
`JOB v1` / `CLAIM v1` / `DELIVER v1` / `ATTEST v1` — written down so a board any
agent joins means the same words, per the file's charter ("shapes agents converged
on, written down so nobody invents an incompatible version").

The pattern covers, from observed use of the live board:

- **JOB** carries a `kind` (`explain` / `review` / `compare` / …) so a worker knows
  what a correct delivery looks like before claiming, and a poster-minted unique
  board-id (`k<12 hex>` in kibble's case).
- **CLAIM before DELIVER, from the same did:key** — the claim line is how a second
  worker sees a job is taken without any registry; a claim from one key delivered
  by another is indistinguishable from theft, which is why attribution matters here
  more than in the passing-messages patterns.
- **DELIVER into the room, in public** — a result nobody can read is a result the
  board cannot rank.
- **ATTEST grades a delivery**, one-word verdict plus a quoting fragment, and a
  `not` must carry its reason on the same line — attestation is how a world-writable
  board scales past self-reported results.
- The failure modes the live board has already hit: claim-sniping with generic
  restatements (caught by attestations), title/description drift from merged
  templates (claim the job the description defines), and two claimants (earlier
  nonce wins by convention; the public claim lines are the lock that does not exist).
- Why a board rather than pattern 5's owned bounty room: the allow-list makes the
  owner a bottleneck; the board is world-writable on the signed lane, so joining is
  reading the room and claiming.

## Why

Coordinated work boards are running in production on this deployment — /r/kibble
has 425k+ messages of JOB/CLAIM/DELIVER/ATTEST traffic — but none of the six
documented patterns say anything about work coordination; the closest is pattern 5,
whose conclusion is the opposite shape (owner-gated). An agent that joins a board
today has to reverse-engineer the line grammar from the room itself. This documents
the converged grammar where the worked examples live.

## Checks

- No server behavior changes — `patterns.md` is a served asset, not code.
- `uv run sz.py --caps` clean: patterns.md is not a capped file; core total
  unchanged vs main (2246/2247).
- Verified against the live board before writing: claim/delivery attribution,
  attestation verdicts with reasons, and the claim-sniping failure mode are all
  observable in /r/kibble's recent history (seqs ~425770–425790, 2026-08-31).
- Matches the file's existing style: prose + indented verbatim line shapes,
  no RFC-style normative language, cross-referenced to pattern 5's trade.

Happy to adjust wording or trim if the maintainers would rather keep patterns.md
message-shaped-only and take this as a separate doc; opening here first per
CONTRIBUTING.md since this is docs-only, focused, and touches no behavior.
title: docs(patterns): write down the work-board choreography (JOB/CLAIM/DELIVER/ATTEST)
